extra.message: Hardcoded Flask Session Secret Key — Full session forgery; attacker can impersonate any user including admins; complete authentication bypass. [verified: app.secret_key is hardcoded as 'super secret key' (app.py line 12) with no environment variable override present in the file, making the Flask session signing key trivially known and enabling complete session forgery for any account.]

Hardcoded Weak Flask Secret Key — Attacker can forge valid Flask session cookies to impersonate any user, including admin accounts, achieving full account takeover [verified: app.py line 12 hardcodes app.secret_key = 'super secret key' as a literal string with no environment-variable override, allowing any attacker who knows this publicly visible key to forge Flask session cookies and impersonate arbitrary users including admins.]

Server-Side Template Injection via request.path in 404 Handler — Unauthenticated remote code execution — attacker can execute arbitrary Python/OS commands via Jinja2 template evaluation [verified: Same as idx 0 — request.path is interpolated via f-string directly into render_template_string at app.py:30-32 with no sanitization or encoding, enabling unauthenticated SSTI/RCE on any 404-triggering request.]

Privilege Escalation Surface — is_admin Exposed in AccountForm — Any user can self-assign admin role by including is_admin=true in the account update POST [verified: The is_admin BooleanField in AccountForm is mass-assigned directly to the user model via current_user.__dict__.update(form.data) in routes/account.py with no privilege check, and the route lacks @login_required so even unauthenticated users can POST is_admin=true to self-escalate. No server-side control filters this field before application to the model.]

Missing Authentication on Account Update Route — Unauthenticated attackers can modify account properties (including is_admin) without any session [verified: Confirmed: routes/account.py update_account() at the POST /account route has no @login_required decorator while the GET /account route at line 18 does; unauthenticated requests can invoke account update logic.]

Mass Assignment — Privilege Escalation via is_admin Field — Any user (even unauthenticated) can escalate to admin by posting is_admin=true, gaining full administrative privileges [verified: Duplicate of findings 2/3 — POST /account lacks @login_required and applies all AccountForm fields including is_admin to current_user.__dict__ then persists via session.merge(); unauthenticated or authenticated privilege escalation to admin is confirmed.]

Privilege Escalation via Mass Assignment of is_admin — Any authenticated user can grant themselves admin privileges by POSTing is_admin=true to /account, gaining access to all admin-only functionality including invite code management. [verified: update_account() lacks @login_required and AccountForm includes is_admin as a BooleanField; filtered_values includes is_admin and is applied via current_user.__dict__.update(), then persisted with session.merge(), allowing any authenticated user to self-promote to admin.]

Privilege Escalation via Mass Assignment (is_admin field) — Any unauthenticated or authenticated user can grant themselves admin privileges, gaining full access to admin functions including invite code management. [verified: Duplicate of findings 2/3/10/15 — POST /account has no @login_required, is_admin BooleanField in AccountForm is included in filtered_values and applied to current_user via __dict__.update() then session.merge(); privilege escalation confirmed.]

Insecure Deserialization via Pickle Cookie (RCE) — Full remote code execution as the application user on the server, reachable without authentication on every HTTP request. [verified: The before_request hook at routes/account.py calls pickle.loads(b64decode(preferences)) on the raw 'preferences' cookie with no HMAC or signature check. This runs on every request including unauthenticated ones, giving trivial unauthenticated RCE.]

Missing Authentication on /darkmode Route (Amplifies Unauthenticated RCE) — Unauthenticated attackers can trigger the pickle deserialization RCE chain (already found at line 118) without needing any session, achieving remote code execution as the application user. [verified: The /darkmode route at routes/account.py has no @login_required decorator (confirmed in source), and the before_request hook unconditionally calls pickle.loads(b64decode(preferences)) on every request including to /darkmode; this confirms a fully unauthenticated RCE trigger path though the RCE itself exists on all endpoints via before_request.]

Hardcoded weak default credentials in database seed — Trivial unauthorized access to user and admin accounts using publicly known default credentials [verified: db_seed.py lines 17-19 hardcode weak plaintext passwords ('user' and 'admin') for seeded accounts, bcrypt-hashing them at runtime but leaving the originals trivially known from the public repository; this is the same root finding as idx 0, confirming unauthorized access to both user and admin accounts on any deployment of this codebase.]

Missing CSRF Protection on All State-Changing Routes — Attacker can trick authenticated users into making unintended state changes (privilege escalation, note deletion, account modification) via cross-origin requests [verified: Flask-WTF is installed but CSRFProtect is never instantiated, all forms extend bare wtforms.Form instead of FlaskForm, and no csrf_token appears in any template — CSRF protection is entirely absent from all state-changing POST routes including account update (which enables privilege escalation), note creation/deletion, and image upload.]

CSRF on Note Creation and Deletion — Attacker forces authenticated victim to create notes (planting stored XSS payloads) or silently deletes arbitrary notes by ID (CSRF + IDOR combination), enabling data destruction and persistent XSS injection across victim accounts. [verified: NoteForm extends wtforms.Form (not FlaskForm), CSRFProtect is never initialized, WTF_CSRF_ENABLED is never set, and neither POST /notes nor POST /notes/<id>/delete performs any CSRF token validation — no compensating control exists anywhere in the codebase. A cross-origin page can silently create or delete notes on behalf of any authenticated user.]

SQL Injection via Search Parameter — Attacker can exfiltrate all notes (including private ones from other users), user credentials, and other database contents [verified: Duplicate of finding 1 — request.args.get('search') is directly interpolated into a SQLAlchemy text() fragment with no parameterization; requires authentication (@login_required present) but is a confirmed SQL injection.]

IDOR: Unrestricted Access to Any User's Private Notes — Any authenticated attacker can read all notes (including private notes) of any user in the system by enumerating user IDs. [verified: get_personal_notes() has @login_required but no ownership check — it queries Note.user_id == user_id where user_id comes from the URL path parameter, allowing any authenticated user to read any user's private notes.]

IDOR — Unauthenticated Access to Other Users' Notes — Any authenticated user can read all private notes belonging to any other user, exposing sensitive data [verified: Duplicate of finding 4 — @login_required is present but there is no ownership check comparing user_id to current_user.id; any authenticated user can read any other user's private notes by varying the URL path parameter.]

Missing CSRF Protection on All State-Changing Endpoints — CSRF attacks on any state-changing operation: account takeover, privilege escalation, note deletion, and more by tricking an authenticated admin or user to visit an attacker-controlled page. [verified: AccountForm extends wtforms.Form (not flask_wtf.FlaskForm), no CSRFProtect(app) call exists anywhere in the codebase, and no WTF_CSRF_ENABLED setting is present; all state-changing POST endpoints are fully CSRF-vulnerable, enabling cross-site privilege escalation and account modification.]

SQL Injection via Registration Code Field — Attacker can bypass registration code validation, dump the entire database (credentials, notes), or cause data corruption [verified: Identical to idx 0: the same validate_token() f-string interpolation at routes/signup.py lines 15-18 takes user-supplied registration_code form data directly into a SQLAlchemy text() query with no parameterization. The only validator is a min-length(5) check, which does not prevent SQL injection payloads.]

Server-Side Request Forgery via Profile Image URL — Attacker can read internal metadata endpoints, scan internal network services, read local files via file:// scheme, and potentially reach internal services not exposed to the internet. [verified: utils/profile_image.py line 7 calls urlopen(url) directly with the user-supplied URL from form.url.data; the only validation is WTForms DataRequired() and URLField which accepts any valid URL including file://, http://169.254.169.254/, and internal addresses — no scheme allowlist, IP restriction, or SSRF protection exists anywhere in the call chain.]

CSRF on Login Form (Login CSRF) — A victim visiting an attacker-controlled page is silently logged into the attacker's account; any data the victim creates (notes, profile info) is immediately accessible to the attacker; chains with stored XSS if attacker pre-planted payloads in their own account. [verified: LoginForm extends plain wtforms.Form (not flask_wtf.FlaskForm), CSRFProtect is never initialized anywhere in the app, and no CSRF token field or manual validation exists in the /login handler — a cross-origin POST will be accepted unconditionally. Login CSRF is confirmed, though its practical impact is limited to session-swap attacks (victim must be tricked into visiting attacker's page while unau]

Insecure Cookie Flags on Preferences Cookie — Cookie can be read by injected JavaScript (XSS chaining), transmitted over unencrypted connections, and used in cross-site request forgery attacks. [verified: response.set_cookie('preferences', ...) is called without httponly=True, secure=True, or samesite flags anywhere in routes/account.py; given the XSS and pickle RCE vulnerabilities present, the absence of HttpOnly meaningfully amplifies the attack surface.]

Insecure cookie flags on preferences cookie (no HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite) — JavaScript can read/overwrite the preferences cookie enabling XSS-to-RCE escalation; cookie transmitted over plaintext HTTP [verified: Duplicate of findings 5/12/18/25 — preferences cookie confirmed set without HttpOnly, Secure, or SameSite in both toggle_darkmode and after_request; absence of HttpOnly enables JavaScript access to a pickle-payload cookie, amplifying XSS-to-RCE.]

No Rate Limiting on Login and Registration Endpoints — Unlimited brute-force of user passwords; mass automated account registration; credential stuffing attacks. [verified: Neither POST /login nor POST /signup implements any rate limiting, CAPTCHA, or lockout; flask-limiter is absent from requirements.txt and no middleware provides throttling, confirming unlimited brute-force and credential-stuffing attacks are possible.]

IDOR — Delete Any Note Without Ownership Check — Any authenticated user can delete notes belonging to other users, causing data loss [verified: The POST /notes/<int:note_id>/delete route (lines 38-51) deletes session.get(Note, note_id) without verifying ownership (note.user_id == current_user.id), so any authenticated user can delete any note by supplying an arbitrary note_id.]

IDOR - Any Authenticated User Can Delete Any Note — Authenticated attacker can delete notes belonging to any other user, including admin notes, causing data loss. [verified: The delete_note() endpoint fetches the note by URL-supplied note_id and calls session.delete(note) with no ownership check against current_user.id; @login_required provides authentication but not authorization.]

Missing Rate Limiting on Signup Endpoint — High-speed automated email enumeration and potential brute-force of invite codes, amplifying the known user enumeration finding. [verified: Confirmed absence of any rate limiting across the entire codebase (no flask_limiter, no custom decorator, no middleware) means the /signup endpoint accepts unlimited automated requests. Combined with the user enumeration vulnerability (distinct 'User already exists' message), an attacker can enumerate all registered emails at high speed; invite code brute-force is a secondary risk given UUID4 code]

Missing Authentication on Darkmode Toggle — Minor: unauthenticated users can set the darkmode preference cookie; this is low severity on its own but contributes to the attack surface. [verified: The /darkmode route has no @login_required decorator, but the impact is limited to an unauthenticated user toggling a preference cookie; on its own this is minor though it contributes to the overall unauthenticated attack surface.]

Unauthenticated Email Disclosure via /is_logged_in — Attacker (or injected XSS payload) can silently harvest authenticated users' email addresses and confirm login status without any credentials. [verified: The /is_logged_in endpoint has no @login_required and returns current_user.email when authenticated; an XSS payload (which exists in this app via stored XSS on notes) running in the victim's browser can fetch this endpoint with credentials and silently harvest the victim's email address and login status.]

Account Enumeration via Registration Error Message and Login Timing — Attacker can enumerate all registered email addresses; enables targeted phishing and credential stuffing. [verified: routes/signup.py line 58 directly confirms existing accounts via a distinct 'User already exists' flash message; the login timing oracle (bcrypt delay vs. immediate 'not found') is a secondary amplifier. Both paths are exposed with zero rate limiting across the entire application.]

User Enumeration via Signup Error Message — Attacker confirms which email addresses are registered, enabling targeted credential stuffing against /login and narrowing phishing targets; especially impactful given the absence of brute-force protection. [verified: routes/signup.py line 58 flashes 'User already exists' exclusively when a submitted email matches an existing account, producing a response distinguishable from other failure modes such as an invalid invite code. No rate limiting or CSRF protection exists on the /signup endpoint, enabling automated enumeration of registered email addresses.]
